name: Multi-Agent Systems
scope: A person with BASIC proficiency level in Multi-Agent Systems as a competency should be able to explain what MAS are, when to use them, and distinguish agents from traditional software objects/services; describe agent properties (autonomy, proactivity, social ability), basic architectures (reactive, deliberative, hybrid, BDI), and agent lifecycles; identify MAS motivations (decentralization, scalability, robustness), use cases (logistics, robotics, LLM orchestration), and trade-offs; understand agent communication (direct/indirect messaging, protocols, ACLs, message schemas), coordination (leader–follower, mediator, task allocation), and failure modes (timeouts, retries, idempotency); model environments (observable, deterministic, static/dynamic, grid/graph), define sensors/actuators, and use simulation tools; implement basic agent behaviors (rule-based, state machines), simple coordination (task sharing, leader election), and have awareness of auctions, voting, and pathfinding; grasp reasoning (rule-based, goal-checking), learning basics (policy adaptation, multi-agent RL concepts), and configure LLM-based agent roles and tools using orchestration libraries; assist in MAS system design (decompose roles, map to code, configure APIs/queues), implement and extend simple agents, wire up communication, and handle basic failures; evaluate MAS using metrics (task completion, throughput, resource use), design simple tests, and use logging/monitoring tools; recognize safety, fairness, and ethical issues (emergent risks, access control, LLM guardrails), and apply basic defensive techniques; use at least one MAS and one LLM-agent framework (e.g., SPADE, JADE, LangChain, CrewAI), configure environments, deploy agents as services/containers, and manage dependencies; read MAS diagrams, document agents, protocols, and environments, follow coding/versioning standards, maintain runbooks, and communicate findings and issues clearly in a team setting.
long_scope:
{"sections":[{"name":"Core Understanding of Multi-Agent Systems","scope_included":"- Understands what a Multi-Agent System (MAS) is and when it is appropriate to use it instead of a single-agent or monolithic system
- Distinguishes clearly between an "agent" and a traditional software object/service (autonomy, proactivity, social ability, situatedness)
- Knows the typical motivations for MAS: decentralization, scalability, robustness, locality of information, modularity, and handling distributed knowledge or control
- Understands the basic components of a MAS: agents, environment, interactions, organizational structures, and global objectives
- Recognizes core MAS paradigms: cooperative vs competitive systems, centralized vs decentralized coordination, loosely vs tightly coupled agents
- Knows the difference between:
  - Multi-agent systems vs distributed systems
  - MAS vs microservices
  - MAS vs multi-threaded programs
- Understands high-level use cases where MAS is commonly applied: logistics, robotics swarms, smart grids, multi-robot coordination, trading/auction systems, simulations, LLM-based assistant teams
- Understands the difference between classical symbolic/BDI agent systems and modern data-driven or LLM-based multi-agent orchestration
- Can articulate both individual agent goals and system-level/global goals and how they may align or conflict
- Understands the concept of emergent behavior: how complex system behavior can arise from relatively simple individual agent rules
- Recognizes the trade-offs of MAS: increased complexity in coordination and debugging vs benefits in flexibility, robustness, and parallelism","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Agent Fundamentals and Architectures","scope_included":"- Understands the concept of an agent lifecycle (perceive → decide → act) and can map code structures to this lifecycle
- Knows basic agent properties: autonomy, reactivity, proactivity, social ability, mobility (conceptual), and rationality (goal-directedness)
- Understands primary agent architecture types:
  - Reactive agents (simple rules, stimulus-response)
  - Deliberative agents (explicit models, planning)
  - Hybrid agents (reactive + deliberative layers)
  - BDI (Belief-Desire-Intention) architecture at a conceptual level
- Can describe the basic elements of BDI agents: beliefs, desires, intentions, plans, and events, and how they relate to agent behavior
- Understands the notion of internal state vs observable state of an agent
- Recognizes concepts of:
  - Goals vs tasks vs roles
  - Capabilities/skills of agents
  - Policies/strategies guiding agent decisions
- Can reason about how to decompose a problem into multiple agents by identifying distinct roles, responsibilities, and knowledge partitions
- Understands the impact of different architectures on:
  - Responsiveness vs optimality
  - Resource usage vs decision quality
  - Ease of implementation vs flexibility
- Can work with simple agent architectures in code (e.g., a loop with perception, decision logic, and action execution) and extend them under guidance
- Knows that agents can be implemented using various underlying technologies (object-oriented classes, services, processes, containers, LLMs as agents) and can map the abstract concept to these concrete realizations","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Agent Communication, Interaction and Coordination Basics","scope_included":"- Understands that interaction is a first-class concept in MAS: agents communicate, coordinate, negotiate, and sometimes compete
- Knows basic interaction modes:
  - Direct messaging (one-to-one, one-to-many)
  - Indirect communication via environment (stigmergy, shared blackboard, shared memory)
  - Publish/subscribe and event-based interaction
- Understands the idea of communication protocols and conversation patterns:
  - Request/response
  - Query/answer
  - Notification/subscribe
  - Simple negotiation patterns (offers, counter-offers, accept/reject)
- Has conceptual awareness of Agent Communication Languages (ACLs) and performatives (e.g., inform, request, propose, agree, refuse), even if not deeply formal
- Can design simple message schemas for agent communication (using JSON, Protobuf, or similar encoding), including:
  - Sender, receiver, conversation ID
  - Message type/performative
  - Payload and context
- Understands the difference between synchronous and asynchronous communication in MAS and their impact on latency, scalability, and complexity
- Knows basic coordination mechanisms:
  - Leader–follower
  - Coordinator/mediator agents
  - Simple task allocation and work queues
  - Turn-taking vs parallel actions
- Understands the concept of shared global state vs local agent state and implications for consistency and conflicts
- Can implement and debug simple communication flows between agents using messaging libraries, HTTP APIs, queues, or MAS frameworks under guidance
- Has awareness of failure modes in agent communication (message loss, delays, duplicates, conflicting messages) and basic strategies to handle them (timeouts, retries, idempotency)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Environment Modeling and Simulation Fundamentals","scope_included":"- Understands the concept of an environment in MAS: the context in which agents perceive and act
- Knows the basic environment classifications:
  - Fully vs partially observable
  - Deterministic vs stochastic
  - Static vs dynamic
  - Discrete vs continuous
- Can define what sensors and actuators mean in software terms (APIs, data streams, environment state access, effectors)
- Can represent simple environments using appropriate data structures (grids, graphs, lists of entities, world state objects)
- Understands the role of a simulation loop or scheduler that advances time, updates environment state, and triggers agent execution
- Recognizes the difference between:
  - Central environment model vs fully distributed representations
  - Simulation-only environments vs real-world-connected environments (IoT, robotics, external APIs)
- Can configure and use basic multi-agent simulation tools or environments for experimentation under guidance
- Understands the concept of time in MAS (discrete time steps vs event-driven vs continuous time) and the implications for agent decision frequency
- Knows how environment constraints and rules influence agent behavior and system-level outcomes
- Understands how to introduce simple randomness into the environment for robustness testing while keeping experiments reproducible (seeds, random distributions)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Basic Multi-Agent Behaviors, Strategies and Algorithms","scope_included":"- Understands fundamental local behavior types:
  - Rule-based behaviors (if-then rules based on local perception)
  - Threshold-based decisions (act when condition exceeds a value)
  - Simple state machines (finite-state agents)
- Can implement simple coordination behaviors:
  - Task sharing via queues or shared data structures
  - Basic work-stealing or load distribution patterns
  - Simple leader election (fixed leader, pre-configured)
- Understands high-level cooperative patterns:
  - Division of labor (different agents responsible for different tasks)
  - Redundancy (multiple agents capable of same task for robustness)
  - Sequential vs parallel workflows across agents
- Has conceptual awareness of basic multi-agent decision concepts:
  - Local vs global objectives
  - Nash equilibrium and basic game-theoretic intuition (without formal derivations)
  - Social welfare vs individual utility
- Understands that conflicting agent objectives can lead to coordination issues (deadlocks, livelocks, inefficiencies) and can identify such issues in simple scenarios
- Can work with basic pathfinding or navigation in multi-agent contexts (e.g., independent pathfinding with awareness of collisions or contention) under guidance
- Has introductory awareness of:
  - Auctions and simple allocation mechanisms (e.g., one-round bidding)
  - Voting or consensus at a conceptual level (majority vote, simple aggregation of preferences)
- Can create and adjust simple local rules to produce desired group behaviors, with support from more experienced team members","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Reasoning, Learning and LLM-based Multi-Agent Orchestration (Basic Level)","scope_included":"- Understands the concept of agent reasoning:
  - Rule-based reasoning (condition-action rules)
  - Simple goal checking (is goal satisfied? what sub-goals remain?)
- Has basic understanding of how learning can occur in MAS:
  - Individual agents adapting policies over time
  - System-level performance feedback informing agent adjustments
- Has introductory familiarity (conceptual) with:
  - Multi-agent reinforcement learning as a family of methods for agents learning from interaction
  - Centralized training vs decentralized execution ideas at a high level
- Can use or extend simple policies provided by others (e.g., heuristic policies, configuration-driven rules) for agents
- Understands the idea of role specialization in agent teams (planner, executor, critic, tool-user, information searcher)
- Has foundational understanding of LLM-based multi-agent systems:
  - LLM instances acting as agents with distinct system prompts, roles, or tools
  - A coordinator or orchestrator controlling agent calls and information flows
  - Shared memory or blackboard for agents to read and write intermediate results
- Can configure basic LLM agent roles and interaction patterns using common orchestration libraries under guidance (e.g., defining tools, setting system messages, specifying routing logic at a high level)
- Understands that LLM-based agents can be non-deterministic and must be constrained via prompts, tools, and validation layers
- Recognizes limitations and common failure patterns of LLM agents (hallucinations, overly verbose responses, forgetting context) and basic mitigation ideas (tool grounding, stricter prompts, shorter contexts)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"System Design and Implementation Tasks for Basic MAS Practitioners","scope_included":"- Can assist in decomposing a problem into multiple agents by:
  - Identifying distinct roles and responsibilities
  - Proposing candidate agents and mapping them to code modules or services
  - Listing the information each agent needs and what it produces
- Can implement simple agents according to an existing architecture or framework:
  - Implementing perception, decision, and action methods provided by a base class or interface
  - Configuring agent parameters (timeouts, thresholds, heuristics)
  - Adding logging and basic state tracking per agent
- Can design and implement straightforward agent interaction flows:
  - Request–response or query–answer patterns
  - Sequential pipelines of agents transforming data
  - Broadcasting updates to a group of agents via a shared channel
- Can extend a small MAS by adding new agent types or behaviors while preserving the existing contract for communication and environment interaction
- Can wire up a MAS to simple external systems:
  - REST or gRPC APIs as environment inputs/outputs
  - Message queues or pub/sub systems as communication channels
  - File or database-backed shared state for coordination
- Can implement LLM-based agent workflows under guidance:
  - Define agent prompts and roles
  - Attach simple tools (e.g., code execution, web/API calls) to agents as supported by frameworks
  - Configure orchestration flows (round-robin, turn-taking, or planner–worker patterns)
- Can implement basic failure handling:
  - Timeouts and retries for agent calls
  - Fallback behaviors when an agent cannot complete a task
  - Simple circuit-breaker-like logic (disable misbehaving agents temporarily)
- Can instrument the system with basic logging and metrics at the agent and system levels to support debugging and evaluation
- Understands and follows established coding standards for agent implementation (naming, structure, separation of concerns between agent logic, communication, and environment modeling)","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Evaluation, Metrics and Testing for Multi-Agent Systems (Basic Level)","scope_included":"- Understands why MAS require both individual-agent and system-level evaluation
- Can identify and track basic metrics, such as:
  - Task completion rate and time
  - Throughput and latency of agent interactions
  - Resource utilization across agents (CPU, memory, API calls)
  - Simple robustness metrics (success under random perturbations)
- Knows how to design simple test scenarios:
  - Fixed environment configurations for reproducible tests
  - Basic stress scenarios (increased number of tasks, simple noise)
- Can create small-scale experiments to compare parameter settings or behavior rules (e.g., changing thresholds, number of agents, or communication intervals)
- Can write and run unit tests for individual agents:
  - Testing decision logic given fixed perceptions
  - Verifying that actions conform to expected formats and constraints
- Can assist in writing integration tests for subsets of agents interacting through a mocked or simplified environment
- Has basic understanding of:
  - Determinism vs stochasticity in MAS simulations and how random seeds impact reproducibility
  - Logging and tracing across agents to reconstruct execution flows
- Can help build simple dashboards or reports that summarize key MAS metrics over time using common monitoring or visualization tools as defined by the team
- Understands limitations of small-scale tests and knows when to escalate to more advanced evaluation (scalability tests, adversarial situations) handled by more experienced team members","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Robustness, Safety, Ethics and Governance (Awareness Level)","scope_included":"- Understands at a conceptual level the risks of decentralized behavior:
  - Unintended emergent behaviors
  - Feedback loops and cascades
  - Deadlocks, livelocks, and oscillations
- Is able to recognize and flag potential safety hazards in MAS designs:
  - Agents taking actions without sufficient supervision in high-stakes domains
  - Conflicting objectives leading to harmful or wasteful behavior
- Has awareness of fairness and bias issues in agent teams, particularly when using data-driven or LLM-based agents
- Understands the importance of:
  - Access control and authorization for agents interacting with sensitive data or powerful tools
  - Rate limiting and resource usage controls on agents (especially for external API calls)
- Can apply basic guardrails in LLM-based multi-agent setups under guidance:
  - Content filters and safety prompts
  - Verifier/critic agents checking outputs for safety or policy compliance
  - Human-in-the-loop checkpoints for critical decisions
- Knows simple defensive design techniques:
  - Whitelisting allowed actions or tools for each agent
  - Validating inputs and outputs at boundaries (schemas, ranges, consistency checks)
- Recognizes when a scenario likely requires advanced safety analysis or domain expert review and escalates appropriately","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Tooling, Frameworks and Platforms for Multi-Agent Systems (Basic Usage)","scope_included":"- Has working familiarity (installation, basic usage) with at least one classical MAS framework or library and one LLM-based multi-agent orchestration framework, as defined by the team
- For classical or symbolic MAS frameworks (depending on stack), can:
  - Understand the basic project structure and configuration model
  - Define agent types/classes and their behaviors
  - Configure communication channels and environment integration
  - Run, monitor, and stop simulations or deployments
- For LLM-based multi-agent frameworks and orchestration libraries, can:
  - Define agent roles, prompts, and simple tools
  - Configure interaction patterns (planner–worker, debate, critic, router)
  - Connect to LLM providers (API keys, model selection, basic configuration)
- For simulation and environment platforms, can:
  - Configure simple grid-based or scenario-based environments
  - Add or remove agents
  - Change environment parameters (e.g., number of tasks, noise levels) for experiments
- For communication and integration tooling, can:
  - Use messaging systems (queues, topics) to connect agents
  - Configure simple routing or topic subscriptions
  - Work with HTTP-based or RPC-based agent APIs
- Can use standard development and debugging tools effectively in a MAS context:
  - Logs filtered by agent ID, time, or conversation
  - Basic distributed tracing if available
  - Breakpoints or interactive debugging for agent logic
- Understands deployment basics for MAS components:
  - Packaging agents as services, containers, or functions
  - Using configuration files or environment variables for parameters
  - Simple scaling of agents (horizontal replication) under guidance
- Follows project conventions for dependency management, versioning, and environment setup across MAS components","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Collaboration, Documentation and Working Practices in MAS Projects","scope_included":"- Can read and understand existing MAS architecture diagrams showing agents, environment, and communication channels
- Can contribute to and maintain up-to-date documentation for:
  - Agent responsibilities and contracts (inputs, outputs, assumptions)
  - Message schemas and interaction protocols
  - Environment specifications and configuration parameters
- Documents new or modified agents with:
  - Purpose and role within the system
  - Key decision rules or policies
  - Configurable parameters and their effects
- Collaborates effectively with more senior team members on MAS design:
  - Participates in design reviews and asks clarifying questions about agent roles and interactions
  - Raises concerns about ambiguity in responsibilities or overlapping roles
- Adheres to agreed coding standards and architectural guidelines for MAS (module boundaries, layering between logic, communication, and environment)
- Uses version control practices suited to MAS projects:
  - Branching strategies for multi-component changes
  - Meaningful commit messages referencing affected agents or flows
- Helps maintain basic runbooks or playbooks for MAS operations:
  - How to start, stop, and monitor the system
  - Known failure modes and simple recovery procedures
- Communicates test findings and experiment results clearly:
  - Summarizes observed system-level behaviors
  - Highlights unexpected or emergent behaviors to the team
- Works effectively in cross-functional teams (data scientists, ML engineers, software engineers, domain experts) by explaining MAS concepts at a basic but accurate level and incorporating feedback into designs and implementations","is_non_core_section":true}]}
